title: Aboriginal Sydney
text: Places with historical associations for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Sydney, from first contact around the harbour to the fight for civil rights in Redfern. Each story is told on Barani, the City of Sydney's Aboriginal history site.
caveat: Only the places that stand in or beside a building today appear on the map; many others are shores, parks and streets.

title: Places of worship
text: Churches, synagogues, mosques and temples. St Mary's Catholic Cathedral and the Great Synagogue look onto Hyde Park, St Andrew's Anglican Cathedral stands beside the Town Hall, and the inner suburbs keep the churches, temples and mosques of the communities that settled around them.

title: The corner pub
text: Sydney's pubs are often called hotels: licensing laws long required them to offer rooms. In the inner city many stand on street corners, built for the terraces and warehouses around them.

title: Developing Sydney, 1900–1920
text: Photographs from the City of Sydney Archives of a city being rebuilt, 1900–1920. In the Archives' words, they inadvertently capture the largely working-class neighbourhoods and people displaced by commercial and government redevelopment. These are the buildings that stand where the photographs were taken.
caveat: A building here stands at a place the City's photographers recorded; it is usually not the building in the photograph, which was often demolished.

source.label: City of Sydney Archives, Developing Sydney 1900–1920, CC BY 4.0

73351.name: Pitt Street Sydney, circa 1901
73351.story: Johnston’s Hotel was on the corner of Pitt and Wilmot streets in the centre of the city. Two men are deep in conversation out the front, while a boy in a cap watches them from a window above. Rugs are airing on the sills. Note the elaborate gas lamps at the pub’s entrances. Publicans were required to have a light burning outside their premises from 1830.

68952.name: George Street Sydney, circa 1901
68952.story: The Canadian Dining Rooms offered a bed for the night, and meals for 4d. The single-storey building near the corner of Regent Street had 18 rooms. The restaurant and boarding house was run by Austin Clarke in 1901, but women ran it previously: Isabella Hawke in the 1890s and Mary Mondrion in 1900. The building was demolished in 1902.

75282.name: Anthony Hordern Palace Emporium fire, George Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75282.story: On 10 July 1901, a ferocious fire swept through Anthony Hordern’s Palace Emporium at Haymarket, near Central Station. The department store, which covered an entire city block, was reduced to cinders within two hours, leading to the loss of five lives and the destruction of more than half a million pounds worth of merchandise. This fire led to better firefighting services for Sydney and regulations

73479.name: Goulburn House, Druitt and Kent streets Sydney, circa 1901
73479.story: Goulburn House on the southeast corner of Druitt and Kent streets offered ‘board and residence’. This elegant building was previously a pub named the Goulbourn Hotel in the 1880s. Sydney Town Hall dominates the horizon behind. An election poster fixed to the cast iron balcony reads ‘Don’t Forget CHUCK’. Captain J A Chuck was a candidate in the Lang Division of the 1901 state election.

88705.name: Crown Studios fire, Market and George streets Sydney, 1918
88705.story: Mark Blow’s Crown Studios was the largest photographic company in Sydney in the 1890s, employing 82 operators, assistants and artists. This photograph, taken from the Queen Victoria Building, shows the aftermath of a massive fire that engulfed the studios and surrounding buildings in December 1918. Fifty returned soldiers helped to fight the blaze, and the proprietor of Roberts Hotel managed to re

75409.name: Albion Street Surry Hills, circa 1902
75409.story: George and Margaret Stebbing and their five children leased this four-roomed timber cottage with a slate shingle roof from the mid-1890s until the turn of the century. Many residents in this part of Surry Hills were renters. Most of the houses on Albion Street were part of the Fosterville Estate, owned by Edward Joseph Sparke. This cottage was pulled down by 1907.

88840.name: Forbes Street Woolloomooloo, circa 1901
88840.story: This view, most likely taken from Forbes Street in Woolloomooloo, shows St Mary’s Cathedral and the ridgeline of Macquarie Street in the far distance. In the foreground, a small derelict cottage with a deeply pitched roof is surrounded by open space. This is in contrast to the surrounding densely-packed terraces, characteristic of the suburb as it developed in the 19th century.

75284.name: Christ Church St Laurence School, Pitt Street Haymarket, circa 1902
75284.story: Perfectly proportioned, the Christ Church St Laurence School was situated on Pitt Street near the corner of Gipps Street (now Gipps Street). The school was designed by architect Edmund Blacket and completed in 1845. It was demolished 60 years later to make way for the approaches to Central Station. A new school was rebuilt nearby, on a smaller footprint, in 1907.

90209.name: Windmill Street Millers Point, circa 1907
90209.story: McBride's Hotel was situated on Windmill Street in Millers Point, overlooking Towns Wharf. Milton Terrace on Lower Fort Street can be seen on the horizon. The hotel had been there since at least the 1860s and remained in-situ until about 1910. This waterfront area was obliterated with the construction of Hickson Road and associated stores and wharfage at Walsh Bay between 1906 and 1922.

89374.name: Church Hill Sydney, circa 1907
89374.story: A woman wearing a long skirt sweeps down Lang Street, towards the Grosvenor House boarding establishment. Behind her are warehouses for Allt & Co and Holdsworth Macpherson, wholesale ironmongers. Burroughs and Watt’s made billiard tables in their three-storey factory, which can be seen in the middle distance. Note the ornate gas lamp on the corner.

75301.name: George Street Haymarket, circa 1912
75301.story: If you peer closely, you will see an inscription on the pediment revealing these were the City Buildings dating to 1876. A man with a large ruler stands above the awning of Horton & Co’s Haymarket Seed Warehouse at number 734. Hortons had an exclusive agreement to market Kentia Palm seeds, plants and ferns imported from Lord Howe Island.

89361.name: Macquarie Place Sydney, circa 1907
89361.story: This view north along Macquarie Place takes in a warehouse built by ex-convict entrepreneur Simeon Lord. By 1907, a number of commercial tenants occupied the building, including a branch of the Bank of NSW. Photographic firm Ward and Farran’s ran the Exchange Studios on the upper level, but had moved out in 1903. The century-old warehouse was demolished in 1908.

69766.name: Missenden and Parramatta roads Camperdown, circa 1912
69766.story: The façade of Thomas Skelly’s produce store is covered with theatre posters and advertisements for Sunol tobacco, Orkney Whisky and Van Houten's Cocoa. A fire broke out in the factory next door in January 1911 and burned down Skelly’s stable and the sulky inside it. Skelly had to move when his rented property was resumed, but he later bought his own shop nearby.

67768.name: Queen Street Chippendale, circa 1912
67768.story: A house-proud woman cleans the front of a large dwelling at 24 Queen Street, Chippendale. A sign in the window is for ‘R Taylor, painter & paperhanger’. Richard Taylor and his family were owner-occupiers. The buildings next door were unfit for human habitation and council served a notice on Henry Childs, the absentee landlord. He remained unresponsive and his buildings were demolished in 1912.

88730.name: Pitt Street Sydney, circa 1912
88730.story: The building at 247A Pitt Street was used as auction rooms by John P Lister for almost 20 years. Lister's Auction Mart attracted big city crowds, who swarmed to hear him 'hold forth'. Kerr and Bingham were high class tailors next door at 247B Pitt Street, and dressed their window with draped fabrics. Both buildings were demolished in 1912.

75307.name: Campbell Street Surry Hills, circa 1913
75307.story: These dwellings near the corner of Elizabeth Street were below street level. In May 1910, Tiy Sun, tenant at 63 Campbell Street, wrote to council because the front room flooded when it rained. Water came in through the door, open fireplaces and ceiling. The roof was still leaking in 1913. The buildings were demolished when Thomas Durack’s Newmarket Hotel on the right was rebuilt and extended.

74123.name: Stanley Street East Sydney, circa 1912
74123.story: Kids play on the street out the front of a half-demolished cottage, once occupied by A Pointing. The steep incline of Stanley Street would have been perfect for wheelbarrow and billycart races. A woman looks down from the balcony of Charles H Grigg’s grocery shop on one side. Mrs Fanny Usher sold secondhand clothes from her shop on the right.

88658.name: Elizabeth Street Sydney, circa 1913
88658.story: Lucretia and Florence Wilton established the Select Registry at 29 Elizabeth Street in 1905. Other employment agencies in the same patch included Alfred Israel’s Inter-State Servants Office and Ryan & Co Labour Agents. Female domestic servants hired from registries and exchanges worked in private homes, boarding houses and hotels. Their hours were long, the work was physically gruelling and the pa

73289.name: Fox’s Buildings, Pitt and Goulburn streets Sydney, circa 1902
73289.story: This panorama, composed from two separate glass plates, shows the northwest intersection of Pitt and Goulburn streets around 1902. Tall cranes in the distance are busy constructing Anthony Hordern & Son’s enormous new retail emporium on Brickfield Hill. A number of Chinese businesses, factories and lodging houses rented shopfronts in Fox’s Buildings opposite, including Quan Hing’s store and Kwong

74820.name: Oxford Street Darlinghurst, 1918
74820.story: Two women, one with a suitcase, deep in conversation on Oxford Street. Behind them is a shoe shop. Next to that is Miss Bermingham, a successful florist shop run by Mary Black and her brother Percy Bermingham from 1894. The shopfront was documented on 16 October 1918, just before the building underwent extensive renovations.

89601.name: Margaret Street and Clarence Lane Sydney, 1918
89601.story: This was a steep, sharp and dangerous intersection. The faded signs on the old corner building indicate it was once a ‘residential chambers’ offering ‘good clean beds’. Perhaps itinerant waterside workers lodged here. It was the middle of winter when this photograph was taken, and women can be seen scavenging timber. A gas lamp in the immediate foreground lighted the way to the Burwood Hotel, oppo

89414.name: Hunter and O'Connell streets Sydney, 1919
89414.story: When this corner building was captured by the camera on 19 February 1919, Sydney was in the midst of an outbreak of the deadly ‘Spanish’ influenza pandemic. The requirement to wear a mask in public was enforced by police. Not all obeyed this command. The two young men outside Horwood & Co have slipped their masks off. The windows of Lubrano & Ferrari are marked with crosses.

69610.name: Fowlers Pottery, Parramatta Road Camperdown, 1920
69610.story: Fowlers Pottery was a family business started by Enoch Fowler in 1837, and taken over by his son Robert in 1879. Production moved to Camperdown in the 1850s, with kilns and chimneys peppering the two hectare site on Parramatta Road. Fowlers produced a range of goods including ginger beer bottles, paving bricks and oven tiles, but their speciality was drainpipes.

75348.name: Campbell Street Surry Hills, 1901
75348.story: A child and kangaroo in the backyard of a small timber semi, owned by Polish-born merchant Adolphus Rogalsky. In May 1901, the occupant wrote to council asking for inspectors to call because the house was ‘getting into a very unsatisfactory condition’ due to landlord neglect. The inspection was carried out on 8 June and this photograph was taken five days later.

88287.name: Church Street Pyrmont, circa 1901
88287.story: A woman stands next to a timber lean-to at the back of a 5-roomed stone cottage at 1 Church Street, Pyrmont. This street was at the tip of Pyrmont peninsula, overlooking Jones Bay. The backyard is a quarried sandstone platform, typical of the geological landform of this area. In 1902, the council issued an order for the tenant and owner to demolish the building.

89314.name: Domain Baths, Woolloomooloo, circa 1908
89314.story: The new Municipal Baths at the edge of Woolloomooloo Bay opened in 1908. The enclosed harbour pool was large enough for swimming competitions and carnivals. It boasted a six-tier diving tower that was 54 feet above mean sea level, and a grandstand that accommodated up to 1,700 spectators. Andrew ‘Boy’ Charlton Pool was built in its place in 1966.

75165.name: Fruit and vegetable markets, Haymarket, circa 1920
75165.story: In 1908, Sydney Municipal Council resumed terrace houses, mills and workshops spread over four acres bounded by Ultimo, Thomas, Hay and Quay streets. The site was cleared to make way for two new market buildings designed by the City Architect. The first market building opened in 1909 and the second in 1910. Additional market buildings were constructed in the area until 1938.

75162.name: Hay and Sussex streets Haymarket, circa 1902
75162.story: A man lounges against a telegraph pole on the corner of Hay and Sussex streets. Behind him are Middleton & Co furniture auction mart and Ah Hang’s furniture repair workshop. Further along Sussex Street are a blacksmiths, farrier and stables. The roofline of the John Bridge woolstore is in the distance. The Great Western Coffee Palace was built here in 1913–1914.

88302.name: Pyrmont Powerhouse, Pyrmont, 1919
88302.story: The council built Pyrmont Powerhouse in 1904 to supply electric lighting to Sydney’s streets, and eventually to provide electricity inside the home. The power station, designed by Brodrick and his chief assistant Merriman, ‘went through several cycles of rebirth, as boilers, turbines, generators and chimneys were replaced and output increased’. Pyrmont Powerhouse increased from its original capaci

75006.name: Hippodrome, Haymarket, circa 1914
75006.story: Belmore Markets, designed by City Architect George McRae, was built in 1893. When new fruit and vegetable markets were built further south in 1908–09, the building was converted into a circus venue for Wirth Bros. The original single-storey structure was carefully dismantled and the ground floor, with its distinctive arches, was elevated to the second storey. The new Hippodrome was completed by 19

74845.name: Municipal Shops, Oxford Street Darlinghurst, 1920
74845.story: Sydney Municipal Council resumed the northern side of Oxford Street, between Liverpool and Bourke streets, in 1909. Over the next five years, buildings were demolished and the street was widened from 18.3 metres to 30.5 metres. The council oversaw the construction of the Municipal Shops, which provided commercial outlets at street level and professional chambers above. This photograph was taken in

68709.name: Quaker cemetery and Friends Meeting House, Devonshire Street Haymarket, circa 1901
68709.story: The Friends Meeting House was built in 1868 within the Quaker section of the Devonshire Street Cemetery. This plain and unpretentious building was in a prominent position opposite the original Redfern Railway Station. A replacement meeting house was built on Devonshire Street in Surry Hills in 1903.

75559.name: Belmore Police Barracks yards and outbuildings, Garden Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75559.story: Apart from providing police accommodation, the barracks included stores where clothing was issued to the 2000 policemen stationed across NSW. There was an amory and armorer’s shop, a service magazine, storage for up to four police vans known as ‘Black Marias’, stabling for 30 horses, drill sheds and a gymnasium.

75557.name: Belmore Police Barracks, Garden Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75557.story: Rear elevation of the Belmore Police Barracks. Buildings from Anthony Hordern’s Haymarket department store are at far left, and the dome of Queen Victoria Building and clocktower of Sydney Town Hall can be seen in the distance. This was one of the first buildings to go, and by July 1901 had been completely demolished.

88606.name: Pastoral Chambers, George Street Sydney, 1908
88606.story: The Pastoral Chambers at 375 George Street, shortly before demolition in 1908. The building was once home to photographic suppliers Baker & Rouse, who were the Kodak representatives in Australia. The Photographic Society of NSW used the rooms upstairs for meetings and exhibitions. The crowd on the street is looking through the windows of Baker & Rouse’s new store next door.

75419.name: Convent of the Good Samaritan, Pitt Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75419.story: The convent and chapel of the Sisters of the Order of the Good Samaritan was built in 1871, on the site of the former Carters Barracks. The grand building was designed by architect D W Ryan. The façade featured white steam-pressed bricks and sandstone ornamentation around the windows. The convent moved to Albion Street in 1903, and the associated school relocated to Glebe.

75556.name: Residence for Inspector General of Police, Pitt Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75556.story: The Residence for Inspector General of Police was occupied by Captain John McLerie (1856–1874) and Edmund Fosbery (1874–c1901). The building was earlier known as the Commandant's Quarters, and had been occupied by Colonel William Lonsdale in the 1830s, followed by Major Joseph Long Innes.

75543.name: Benevolent Society’s asylum, Pitt Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75543.story: From the earliest days of the colony, the care of infirm and destitute people, including the ageing convict population, was reliant on charitable non-government organisations. The Benevolent Society of NSW was founded in 1813 with the aim of providing relief and accommodation to paupers, the chronically sick, people with disabilities, single mothers, abandoned children and the aged.

89629.name: Kent Street Millers Point, circa 1901
89629.story: The brick building on the corner of Gas Lane was a factory for Zetz Spa. Mineral spring water from Ballimore, near Dubbo, was bottled here. In March 1900, the business owner J W Cockbaine, also Petersham’s mayor, complained about John Mannix’s ‘lower class boarding house’ next door. Mannix burnt bones and old boots, and kept chickens and ducks that stirred up the yard, causing noxious fumes.

68968.name: Benevolent Society’s asylum, Pitt Street Haymarket, circa 1901
68968.story: The Benevolent Society’s Asylum was built in 1820 to a design by convict-bricklayer Francis Lawless. The imposing building on Pitt Street was demolished to make way for Central Station, although it was still occupied in July 1901. The young boy in the tweed cape is possibly photographer Charles Kent’s son.

89614.name: Kent Street Millers Point, circa 1901
89614.story: This single-storey building with matching dormer windows is perched high on a sandstone wall above Kent Street. A young boy in a sailor suit, possibly the photographer’s son, stands on the steps leading to the entry. This was once a pub known as the Dove and Olive Branch, run by female publican Ann Bushby in the 1840s.

89543.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
89543.story: A group of children are lined up in front of Daniel Giltinan’s cooperage at 220 Kent Street. The cooper’s house, workshop and yard, along with the six terrace houses to the right, were owned by Edward Day. By 1910, there were warehouses here for the Baltic Separator Co, McIlraiths, NSW Produce Co, and Poole & Holmes Merchants.

88565.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
88565.story: This had been William Baldock’s Clarence and Richmond River Hotel from the 1860s. By the turn of the century it was a boarding house run by Mrs M E Millen. It provided 'Lodgings for Respectable Men' for 4d a week. The façade is adorned with election posters and a sign for John Joseph Power, a candidate in the 1901 state election.

88573.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
88573.story: A young boy, possibly the photographer’s son, stands outside a double-storey stone house at 381 Kent Street. The building was used as a boarding house in the late 19th century. It was owned by William Hillas, and later his widow Catherine. The Hillas family had extensive real estate holdings across metropolitan Sydney. The building was demolished and replaced with a warehouse by 1904.

89641.name: Glover’s cottages, Kent Street Millers Point, circa 1901
89641.story: Thomas Glover was a stonemason, publican and ex-convict. He built these stone cottages on Kent Street in the 1820s. When Glover died in 1836, these buildings were inherited by his son James. The single-storey semi-detached cottages to the right were resumed by the NSW Government in 1900 but spared demolition. They were known as ‘The Ark’ because they became stranded from changing street levels.

89637.name: Kent Street Millers Point, circa 1901
89637.story: The timber structure at far left was the workshop of John H Dawson, scull and oar maker. Competitive rowing gained popularity from the 1860s onwards. Richard Green, Ned Trickett and Henry Searle were some of the world-famous champion scullers who trained on Sydney Harbour and used sculls, a type of oar, made by Dawson.

89608.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
89608.story: The three-level rendered brick conjoined building at far right was offered for sale in August 1902. Prospective buyers were told that it was ‘eminently suitable for a store’ because it had access from both Kent Street and Clarence Lane, on two different levels, and was close to the bustling wharves of Darling Harbour. The building was replaced by the Catholic Seamen’s Institute in 1924.

88578.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
88578.story: A small boy gazes from the doorway of 389 Kent Street. These three cottages were owned by Samuel Nisbet Hogg, a bank manager, novelist and amateur historian from Balmain. The compact dwellings were offered for sale in 1901. The workshop at far left was rented by John Close, printers' engineer and machinist. A sign for F Haggett's cooperage can be seen to the right.

88574.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
88574.story: This solid stone building was offered for sale by auction on Thursday 27 September 1900. For over two decades before, it had been a lodging house for single men, many who worked on the nearby wharves. Elizabeth White ran the establishment from the mid-1890s. By 1904 the building was a printing office run by her son Frederick William White.

88548.name: Kent Street Sydney, circa 1901
88548.story: This building was featured in the 1912 publication titled ‘Stories of Old Sydney’, written by Charles H Bertie and illustrated by Sydney Ure Smith. Bertie described the double-storey brick house as 'a relic of old Kent Street', and claimed it was built in the 1820s when the area 'was the dwelling place of old skippers and mercantile men'.

88551.name: Federal Dining Rooms, King and Kent streets Sydney, circa 1901
88551.story: Tom Virgo kept the Federal Dining Rooms at the corner of King and Kent streets. In 1902, a royal commission was held to investigate allegations by Virgo and his wife about their ill treatment by seven policemen. In evidence, a neighbour claimed Virgo's establishment was 'visited by a very low class of people'. Another testified that rooms were let ‘to men and women at all hours of the night'.

90115.name: Trinity Avenue Millers Point, circa 1901
90115.story: This view is south along Trinity Avenue, towards Argyle Street. This had been a section of Upper Fort Street that was renamed in 1899 after the Garrison (Holy Trinity) Church. The houses perched on the hewn sandstone platform were built in the subdivided backyards of residences on Princes Street. The entire street and houses were swallowed up by the approaches to the Sydney Harbour Bridge in the 1

89814.name: Whaler’s Arms Hotel, Gloucester Street The Rocks, circa 1901
89814.story: The Whaler’s Arms Hotel, earlier known as St Patricks Inn, was built on Gloucester Street in 1830 by James and Sarah Byrne. The prominent building incorporated an earlier house built for butcher George Cribb. By 1901, the former hotel was a lodging house run by Mary and Joseph Awlsbury. It was demolished in 1907.

90120.name: Hero of Waterloo Hotel, Lower Fort and Windmill Streets Millers Point, circa 1907
90120.story: There were upwards of 50 hotels trading in The Rocks and Millers Point in the late 19th century. The Hero of Waterloo was built in 1843–44 by George Paton, a Scottish-born master stonemason. The hotel vies for the title of Sydney's oldest continuously trading pub. The rough-cut sandstone walls and heavy timber beams evoke an atmosphere of the rough mariner’s life.

135842.name: Cumberland Place, The Rocks, circa 1912
135842.story: Cumberland Place was built to a design by Colonial Architect Francis Greenway in c1825 for Robert Campbell Snr. It was one of a number of grand houses built at the northern end of Cumberland Street in the 1820s and 30s. This was the childhood home of David Scott Mitchell, book collector and benefactor of the Mitchell Library at the State Library of NSW.

72830.name: Jones Street Ultimo/Pyrmont, circa 1901
72830.story: An end building on Jones Street in Ultimo in the midst of demolition. A sign on the awning is for Mick Curley, Provision Merchant. The wall is painted with advertisements for Siren soap and Bonnington’s Irish Moss. Election posters on the timber hoarding are for George Harris and W H Watt, local candidates in the Denison Division of the 1901 state election.

75280.name: George Street Haymarket, circa 1901
75280.story: This row of commercial buildings on the corner of George Street and Ultimo Road was photographed in 1901, most likely in the aftermath of the destructive fire that destroyed Anthony Hordern’s retailing empire on the opposite side of the road. Windows are smashed, and the sunshades strung up across the ornate cast-iron awnings are tattered and burnt.

89452.name: Bowden's Corner, Hunter and Castlereagh streets Sydney, circa 1907
89452.story: This intersection was known as Bowden’s Corner. Thomas Kite from Bathurst built a city residence here in the 1840s, which later became a pub run by Mrs Bowden. The diminutive corner building was a landmark because a large Norfolk Pine grew through the middle of it, which was used as a coat rack for the hotel patrons. The building and tree were demolished in 1909.

74954.name: Oxford Street Surry Hills, circa 1901
74954.story: Joe Gardiner was known as the ‘Lively Bootman’. The plate glass windows of his store on the corner of Oxford and Riley streets are jam-packed with an array of shoes and boots, all with price tags attached. Gardiner’s shops were all over Sydney, as were his painted advertisements adorning pavements, walls and the frontages of other nearby buildings.

75008.name: George Street Sydney, circa 1901
75008.story: These shopfronts on George Street accommodated a boarding house run by W A Stanton, and jeweller and watchmaker T M Alcock and Son. Adjacent buildings on the corner of Hay Street had been pulled down in February 1900. The vacant site was covered with a hoarding, painted with advertisements for Wolfe’s Schnapps and Bull Dog Stout.

73525.name: Bathurst Street Sydney, circa 1902
73525.story: This lodging house directly opposite St Andrews Cathedral was run by John Simpson, and provided ‘Good Beds for 3’ 6 per week’. Some of the long-term residents can be seen on the porch. Working horses are lined up out the front. The first horse is attached to a sulky, and the one behind is drawing a flat lorry used for deliveries.

75351.name: Smith Street Surry Hills, 1902
75351.story: Three boys and a dog pose for the camera. Freestanding timber cottages like this one with a timber shingle roof, were becoming increasingly rare by the turn of the century. The three-roomed dwelling was occupied by Anne Kennedy from the mid-1890s. All the buildings on the eastern side of Smith Street were part of Edward Joseph Sparke’s Fosterville Estate.

88626.name: King and George streets Sydney, circa 1901
88626.story: A policeman directs traffic at the intersection known as ‘Waters Corner’, named for the ladies outfitters here. This was regarded as one of the busiest and most congested corners for pedestrian traffic in Sydney, prompting complaints about loitering and loafing. A proposal to pull the Waters building down in 1902 was an opportunity to widen the footway. Rebuilding did not eventuate until 1913.

75510.name: Railway Square Haymarket, circa 1904
75510.story: View south from the junction of George and Pitt streets. The spire of Christ Church St Laurence dominates the skyline. The low building in the foreground was the Headquarters of the Civil Ambulance & Transport Brigade of NSW, but was earlier a police watch house. It was replaced with Sydney’s tallest building in 1906, Marcus Clark & Co department store.

68924.name: Irving Street Chippendale, circa 1908
68924.story: View east along Irving Street, looking towards Tooth’s Brewery buildings on Balfour Street. This row of 12 terraces, on the corner of Carlton Street, was eventually swallowed up by the brewery. Children were part of the street life of Chippendale. A nearby landlord complained that it was ‘a terrible street’ and that children were always dirtying and chalking on her house.

74985.name: Brisbane Street Surry Hills, circa 1912
74985.story: This row of double-storey terraces was sold to Sydney Arthur Josephson in November 1911, and he began to demolish them soon after. The building materials being salvaged were auctioned by James Cowan. Tenants in 1912 included Florence Murray, Ah Wong, Ernest Rochester and Annie McClusky. A streetseller hawking his wares can be seen at the top of the street.

74205.name: Palmer Street Darlinghurst, 1917
74205.story: Children pose in front of a ramshackle timber outbuilding at the rear of 170–172 Palmer Street, on the corner of Sutton and Bourke lanes. The photograph was taken on Friday 25 May 1917. In the 1990s, buildings and streets here were obliterated to make way for the Eastern Distributor.

88478.name: Harwood Street Pyrmont, 1917
88478.story: Council resumed buildings along Harwood Street as part of the Pyrmont Bridge Road resumption in the early 20th century. The timber double-storey conjoined terrace at 10–12 Harwood Street is in the process of demolition. The windows are boarded up. One half of the terrace had been a grocery store run by W Fross. Pyrmont locals pick over an empty block of land next door. The dome of the Queen Victor

73328.name: Liverpool and Castlereagh streets Sydney, circa 1912
73328.story: This view along Castlereagh Street takes in an elegant cottage with deep eaves, reputedly the home of William Roberts, one-time alderman on the council and Sydney’s oldest practising solicitor when he died. Squeezed in behind is the Particular Baptist Church and manse. Mark Foy’s landmark Piazza store was directly opposite, which may account for the stylishly-dressed women crossing at this busy co

89936.name: George Street Sydney, circa 1907
89936.story: This long terrace on the corner with Essex Street in The Rocks is notable for its uniform windows on the upper level and the signwriting on the facades. There was a diverse array of occupants including a boot store, pawnbroker, hairdresser, tattooist, refreshment rooms, bird dealer, tobacconist, clothier and a dispensary. The buildings were offered for sale by auction on 27 May 1908.

72849.name: Jones Street Pyrmont, 1919
72849.story: This row of eight brick terraces on the corner of Fig Street was typical of speculative housing built in the 1880s as working class rentals. This photograph was taken on 23 January 1919, just before the houses were demolished to make way for Horman & Wormald’s wool and hide store. That building was in turn demolished to create Fig Lane Park.

75430.name: George Street Sydney, circa 1912
75430.story: Sol Levy and his family manufactured hand-rolled cigars using imported tobacco from the early 1890s. When this photograph was taken, the family-run tobacconist business was in the process of moving next door to number 713, where they remained until 2015. Sol Levy specialised in pipes and cigars, and there was a barber’s saloon on the premises until the early 1990s.

89903.name: Harrington Street The Rocks, 1919
89903.story: Sunday Times Newspaper Co Ltd was the owner of this row of terraces when this photograph was taken on 1 October 1919. The buildings were taken down soon after, and the site was vacant by 1921. It’s possible that the woman in the doorway of 99 Harrington Street is Ellen Valentine with some of her grandchildren. She and husband Joshua rented here from at least 1914.

89571.name: John Keep warehouse, Sussex Street Sydney, 1920
89571.story: Men sit on top of horse-drawn drays lined up along outside the John Keep warehouse on Sussex Street. The drays are piled high with bales and tea chests.

73472.name: George Street Sydney, 1918
73472.story: A woman and a soldier talk on the pavement outside the American Tailoring Depot near the corner of George and Park streets, directly opposite Sydney Town Hall. The building was in the middle of being demolished to make way for an extension to Bebarfald's department store. Sunshades hanging from the awning protect the west-facing shopfronts from the sun.

title: The apartment city
text: New South Wales introduced strata title in 1961, letting the flats of one building be owned one by one. It made inner Sydney a city of apartments, from the walk-up blocks of the 1960s and 70s to the towers of Pyrmont, the city centre and Green Square. Coloured by the decade each strata plan was registered.
caveat: Older buildings converted to strata show their conversion decade.

title: The skyline
text: For most of the twentieth century no building in Sydney could rise above 150 feet, 46 metres. The limit was lifted in 1957, and the towers came: the AMP Building at Circular Quay first, then Australia Square, and a skyline that has kept growing on both sides of the harbour.
